questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the particles of a gas is correct?
options: They are closely packed and vibrate about fixed positions.
They are far apart and move randomly at high speeds.
They are closely packed but slide over one another.
They are at rest when the gas is in a closed container.
questions.explanation: Gas particles are widely separated and in rapid random motion; fixed positions describe solids and sliding layers describe liquids.

questions.topic: Structure of matter (kinetic theory and diffusion)
questions.stem: In a Brownian motion experiment, smoke particles in air are observed to move in a jerky, random way. The motion is caused by
options: the smoke particles attracting one another.
convection currents in the smoke cell.
uneven bombardment of the smoke particles by invisible air molecules.
the heat from the lamp evaporating the smoke particles.
questions.explanation: Air molecules strike each smoke particle unevenly from different sides at any instant, giving it a random, zig-zag path.

questions.topic: Structure of matter (kinetic theory and diffusion)
questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, when the temperature of a fixed mass of gas in a rigid container is raised,
options: the average kinetic energy of the molecules increases, so the pressure increases.
the molecules become larger, so the pressure increases.
the number of molecules increases, so the pressure increases.
the average speed of the molecules is unchanged but the pressure increases.
questions.explanation: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules; faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often, raising pressure at constant volume.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fundamental quantity?
questions.explanation: Electric current (ampere) is one of the seven SI base quantities; force, velocity and pressure are derived.

questions.stem: The S.I. unit of pressure, the pascal, is equivalent to
questions.explanation: Pressure = force/area, so 1 Pa = 1 N m^-2. N m is the unit of work or moment; J s^-1 is the watt.

questions.stem: The dimensions of power are
questions.explanation: Power = work/time = (M L^2 T^-2)/T = M L^2 T^-3. M L^2 T^-2 is energy and M L T^-2 is force.

questions.stem: The period T of oscillation of a mass m on a spring of stiffness k is assumed to be T = c m^x k^y, where c is a dimensionless constant. The values of x and y are
questions.explanation: k has dimensions M T^-2. T^1 = M^x (M T^-2)^y gives x + y = 0 and -2y = 1, so y = -1/2 and x = 1/2, consistent with T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).

questions.stem: The position of a town on the surface of the earth is usually stated by giving its
questions.explanation: Positions on the earth's surface are fixed by the coordinates latitude and longitude.

questions.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the internal diameter of a test tube?
questions.explanation: Vernier calipers have inside jaws for internal diameters and read to 0.01 cm; a micrometer is for small external dimensions.

questions.stem: A micrometer screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and its thimble has 50 divisions. Its least count is
questions.explanation: Least count = pitch / number of thimble divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.

questions.stem: A girl walks 120 m due east and then 50 m due north. The magnitude of her displacement is
questions.explanation: Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish: sqrt(120^2 + 50^2) = 130 m. 170 m is the total distance.

questions.stem: A bearing of 270 degrees corresponds to the direction
questions.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north: 90 is east, 180 south, 270 west.

questions.stem: A body of mass 6 kg is taken from the earth (g = 10 m s^-2) to the moon (g = 1.6 m s^-2). Its mass on the moon is
questions.explanation: Mass is the quantity of matter and does not change with location; only weight changes.

questions.stem: Which of the following instruments measures weight rather than mass?
questions.explanation: A spring balance measures the pull of gravity (a force); beam, chemical and lever balances compare masses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a suitable device for measuring time?
questions.explanation: A hydrometer measures relative density of liquids. Pendulums, stop-watches and quartz clocks rely on a regular repeating motion.

questions.stem: A metal block measures 5 cm by 4 cm by 2 cm and has a mass of 316 g. Its density is
questions.explanation: Volume = 5 x 4 x 2 = 40 cm^3; density = 316/40 = 7.9 g cm^-3.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of two liquids of densities 800 kg m^-3 and 1200 kg m^-3 are mixed. Assuming no change in total volume, the density of the mixture is
questions.explanation: For equal volumes V, density = (800V + 1200V)/2V = 1000 kg m^-3. 960 kg m^-3 would apply to equal masses.

questions.stem: The pressure at a point in a liquid at rest does NOT depend on
questions.explanation: p = h rho g; it depends on depth, density and g but not on the shape or cross-sectional area of the vessel.

questions.stem: A diver is 15 m below the surface of a lake. If atmospheric pressure is 1.0 x 10^5 Pa, the density of water is 1000 kg m^-3 and g = 10 m s^-2, the total pressure on the diver is
questions.explanation: Total pressure = atmospheric + h rho g = 1.0 x 10^5 + 15 x 1000 x 10 = 2.5 x 10^5 Pa.

questions.stem: The height of the mercury column in a simple barometer at a place is 74 cm. If the density of mercury is 13 600 kg m^-3 and g = 10 m s^-2, the atmospheric pressure there is
A solid weighs 2.4 N in air, 1.6 N in water and 1.76 N in a certain oil. The relative density of the oil is
questions.explanation: R.D. of liquid = loss of weight in liquid / loss of weight in water = (2.4 - 1.76)/(2.4 - 1.6) = 0.64/0.80 = 0.80.

questions.stem: A floating body displaces its own
options: density of the fluid in which it floats.
volume of the fluid in which it floats.
weight of the fluid in which it floats.
surface area of the fluid in which it floats.
questions.explanation: Law of flotation: a floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.

questions.stem: A block of wood of density 600 kg m^-3 floats in fresh water of density 1000 kg m^-3. What fraction of its volume is below the water surface?
questions.explanation: Weight = upthrust: rho_wood V g = rho_water V_sub g, so V_sub/V = 600/1000 = 0.6.

questions.stem: A hydrometer floats deeper in liquid X than in liquid Y. It follows that
options: liquid X is denser than liquid Y.
liquid X is less dense than liquid Y.
the upthrust in X is greater than in Y.
the hydrometer is heavier in X than in Y.
questions.explanation: The upthrust equals the hydrometer's weight in both liquids; to displace the same weight of a less dense liquid, it must sink deeper.

questions.stem: The motion of the needle of a sewing machine is best described as
questions.explanation: The needle moves repeatedly up and down about a mean position: oscillatory (vibratory) motion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of rotational motion?
options: The spinning of a ceiling fan blade about its axis
A car moving along a straight road
The movement of smoke particles in air
The swinging of a simple pendulum
questions.explanation: Rotation is motion about a fixed axis; the car is translational, smoke particles random and the pendulum oscillatory.

questions.stem: Two buses travel in the same direction along a straight highway at 72 km/h and 54 km/h. The velocity of the faster bus relative to the slower one, in m/s, is
questions.explanation: Relative velocity = 72 - 54 = 18 km/h = 18 x 1000/3600 = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: A force can do all the following EXCEPT
options: change the shape of a body.
change the direction of motion of a body.
change the mass of a body.
set a body at rest into motion.
questions.explanation: A force can change speed, direction or shape, but it cannot change the quantity of matter in a body.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a field force (a force that acts without contact)?
questions.explanation: Magnetic, electric and gravitational forces act at a distance through a field; friction, tension and reaction are contact forces.

questions.stem: A 20 kg box rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor is 0.35. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the least horizontal force needed to start the box moving is
questions.explanation: Limiting friction = mu R = 0.35 x 20 x 10 = 70 N.

questions.stem: A block is placed on a plane whose angle of inclination is slowly increased. The block just begins to slide when the angle is 31 degrees. The coefficient of static friction is approximately
questions.explanation: At limiting equilibrium on an incline, mu = tan(theta) = tan 31 degrees = 0.60.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of friction?
options: It allows car brakes to stop the vehicle.
It enables us to walk without slipping.
It causes wear and tear of moving machine parts.
It allows a nail to hold firmly in wood.
questions.explanation: Friction wastes energy as heat and wears machine parts; the other options are useful effects of friction.

questions.stem: A steel ball is released in a tall column of glycerine. After falling some distance it moves with a constant velocity because
options: the weight of the ball is balanced by the upthrust and the viscous drag.
the upthrust becomes greater than the weight.
the glycerine becomes less viscous with depth.
questions.explanation: When weight = upthrust + viscous drag, the resultant force is zero and the ball moves at its terminal velocity.

questions.stem: A stone of mass 0.2 kg tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. The tension in the string (neglecting gravity) is
questions.explanation: Centripetal force = m v^2 / r = 0.2 x 16/0.5 = 6.4 N.

questions.stem: A wheel makes 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity is
questions.explanation: 300 rev/min = 5 rev/s; omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 5 = 10 pi rad s^-1.

questions.stem: A keke (tricycle) covers 18 km in 30 minutes. Its average speed in m/s is
Velocity differs from speed because velocity
options: has direction as well as magnitude.
questions.explanation: Velocity is a vector (speed in a specified direction); speed is a scalar.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides 6 km at 12 km/h and then another 6 km at 4 km/h. Her average speed for the whole journey is
questions.explanation: Times are 0.5 h and 1.5 h; average speed = total distance/total time = 12/2 = 6 km/h, not the simple mean of the speeds.

questions.stem: The slope of a displacement-time graph gives the
questions.explanation: Gradient = change in displacement / change in time = velocity.

questions.stem: A displacement-time graph for a body is a straight horizontal line. This shows that the body is
questions.explanation: A horizontal line means the displacement does not change with time: the gradient (velocity) is zero.

questions.stem: A car increases its velocity from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. Its acceleration is
A train accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 40 s, travels at 20 m/s for 120 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 20 s. Its average speed for the whole journey is
questions.explanation: Distance = 400 + 2400 + 200 = 3000 m; total time = 180 s; average speed = 3000/180 = 16.7 m/s.

questions.topic: Equations of motion with constant acceleration
questions.stem: A stone is dropped from the top of a building and hits the ground after 3 s. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the height of the building is
Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Energy has magnitude only; momentum, weight and displacement all have direction.

questions.stem: On a vector diagram, the length of the arrow representing a force indicates the
options: point of application of the force.
questions.explanation: A vector is drawn to scale: its length gives the magnitude and the arrowhead and orientation give direction.

questions.stem: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at a point. Which of the following CANNOT be their resultant?
questions.explanation: The resultant lies between the difference (2 N) and the sum (14 N) of the magnitudes; 16 N is impossible.

questions.stem: Two forces of 10 N and 6 N act at a point with an angle of 60 degrees between them. The magnitude of their resultant is
A canoe that can travel at 4 m/s in still water is paddled straight across a river flowing at 3 m/s. The resultant speed of the canoe relative to the bank is
questions.explanation: The velocities are perpendicular: sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = 5 m/s.

questions.stem: The moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the
options: perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
time for which the force acts.
mass of the body on which it acts.
questions.explanation: Moment = F x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action; unit N m.

questions.stem: A uniform metre rule is balanced at its 50 cm mark. A 30 g mass hangs at the 20 cm mark. At what mark must a 45 g mass be hung to restore balance?
questions.explanation: Anticlockwise moment = 30 x 30 = 900; 45 x d = 900 gives d = 20 cm from the pivot, i.e. the 70 cm mark.

questions.topic: Conditions for equilibrium of rigid bodies
questions.stem: A uniform plank 4 m long and of weight 300 N is supported at its two ends. A boy of weight 500 N stands 1 m from one end, A. The reaction at end A is
questions.explanation: Take moments about the other end B: R_A x 4 = 500 x 3 + 300 x 2 = 2100, so R_A = 525 N (and R_B = 275 N).

questions.stem: A body is in stable equilibrium if, when slightly displaced, its centre of gravity
options: stays at the same height and the body rests in its new position.
falls and the body topples over.
rises and the body returns to its original position.
questions.explanation: In stable equilibrium a small displacement raises the centre of gravity, and the restoring moment returns the body.

questions.topic: Illustration, explanation and definition of simple harmonic motion
questions.stem: A body performs simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is
options: directly proportional to its displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards that point.
constant and directed towards a fixed point.
inversely proportional to its displacement from a fixed point.
directly proportional to its velocity and in the same direction.
questions.explanation: Definition of S.H.M.: a = -omega^2 x, proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.

questions.stem: A particle moves in S.H.M. with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 20 rad s^-1. Its maximum speed is
questions.explanation: v_max = omega A = 20 x 0.05 = 1.0 m s^-1. (Maximum acceleration would be omega^2 A = 20 m s^-2.)

questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem: A simple pendulum has a length of 0.9 m. Taking g = 10 m s^-2 and pi = 3.14, its period is approximately

questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem: The length of a simple pendulum is increased to four times its original value. Its period
questions.explanation: T is proportional to sqrt(L); sqrt(4) = 2, so the period doubles.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 200 N m^-1 oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. The total energy of the oscillation is
Soldiers are ordered to break step when crossing a bridge in order to avoid
questions.explanation: If the marching frequency matched a natural frequency of the bridge, resonance could produce large, damaging oscillations.

questions.topic: First Law: inertia of rest and inertia of motion
questions.stem: Passengers in a bus jerk forward when the bus stops suddenly. This is due to
options: friction between the seat and the passengers.
the reaction of the bus floor.
questions.explanation: Their bodies tend to continue moving forward (Newton's first law) when the bus decelerates.

questions.topic: Second Law: force, acceleration, momentum and impulse
questions.stem: A resultant force of 24 N acts on a body of mass 8 kg. The acceleration produced is

questions.topic: Second Law: force, acceleration, momentum and impulse
questions.stem: A footballer kicks a 0.45 kg ball from rest to a speed of 20 m/s. If his boot is in contact with the ball for 0.05 s, the average force on the ball is
questions.explanation: F = change of momentum / time = 0.45 x 20/0.05 = 180 N.

questions.topic: Second Law: force, acceleration, momentum and impulse
questions.stem: A 60 kg woman stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is accelerating upwards at 2 m s^-2. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the reading of the scale is
questions.explanation: R - mg = ma, so R = m(g + a) = 60 x 12 = 720 N.

questions.topic: Second Law: force, acceleration, momentum and impulse
questions.stem: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick together. Their common velocity after collision is
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: 3 x 4 = (3 + 1)v, so v = 3 m/s.

questions.stem: When a person walks forward, the force that actually pushes the person forward is
options: the force of the foot on the ground.
the frictional force of the ground on the foot.
the normal reaction of the ground.
questions.explanation: The foot pushes backwards on the ground; by Newton's third law the ground pushes forwards on the foot through friction.

questions.stem: In a torchlight powered by dry cells, the energy conversion is
options: chemical to electrical to light and heat.
questions.explanation: The cells convert chemical energy to electrical energy, which the bulb converts to light (and heat).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation: Solar energy is continually replenished; crude oil, coal and natural gas are finite fossil fuels.

questions.stem: The Kainji and Jebba power stations in Nigeria generate electricity mainly from
questions.explanation: Both are hydroelectric stations on the River Niger that convert the potential energy of stored water into electrical energy.

questions.stem: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy
options: can be created from mass in all chemical reactions.
is always lost as heat in every conversion.
can neither be created nor destroyed, but can be changed from one form to another.
is constant in every individual form.
questions.explanation: The total energy of an isolated system is constant; it only changes form.

questions.stem: A 1200 kg car is moving at 15 m/s. Its kinetic energy is
A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Neglecting air resistance and taking g = 10 m s^-2, its speed just before it hits the ground is
questions.explanation: mgh = (1/2)mv^2 gives v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s.

questions.stem: A water pump raises 600 kg of water through a height of 12 m in 2 minutes. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, the useful power output of the pump is
A pulley system with a velocity ratio of 5 lifts a load of 800 N with an effort of 200 N. The efficiency of the system is
A load of 600 N is pushed up a rough inclined plane of length 5 m to a height of 1.5 m using an effort of 250 N parallel to the plane. The efficiency of the plane is
questions.explanation: Work output = 600 x 1.5 = 900 J; work input = 250 x 5 = 1250 J; efficiency = 900/1250 x 100% = 72%.

questions.stem: Mercury is preferred to water as a thermometric liquid because mercury
options: is opaque, expands uniformly and does not wet glass.
has a higher specific heat capacity than water.
freezes at a higher temperature than water.
is colourless and easy to read.
questions.explanation: Mercury is opaque (easily seen), expands fairly uniformly, does not cling to glass and is a good conductor of heat.

questions.stem: A temperature of 37 degrees Celsius on the Kelvin scale is
questions.explanation: T(K) = theta(degrees C) + 273 = 37 + 273 = 310 K.

questions.stem: The length of the mercury thread of an uncalibrated thermometer is 2.0 cm at the ice point and 22.0 cm at the steam point. What temperature corresponds to a thread length of 9.0 cm?
Which of the following is NOT an effect of heat on matter?
questions.explanation: Heating can change temperature, state, volume, pressure or resistance, but not the mass of a body.

questions.stem: A steel rod is 2.000 m long at 20 degrees C. Its linear expansivity is 1.2 x 10^-5 K^-1. The increase in its length when heated to 70 degrees C is
questions.explanation: Delta L = alpha L Delta theta = 1.2 x 10^-5 x 2.000 x 50 = 1.2 x 10^-3 m.

questions.stem: Water is unusual because between 0 degrees C and 4 degrees C it
options: expands on heating, so its density is minimum at 4 degrees C.
contracts on heating, so its density is maximum at 4 degrees C.
boils if the pressure is reduced.
questions.explanation: Anomalous expansion: water contracts from 0 to 4 degrees C, reaching maximum density at 4 degrees C. This is why ponds freeze from the top.

questions.stem: Heat reaches the earth from the sun mainly by
questions.explanation: Space is nearly a vacuum, so only electromagnetic radiation can transfer the energy.

questions.stem: Land breezes blow from land to sea at night because
options: the land cools faster than the sea, so warm air rises over the sea and cooler air from the land replaces it.
the sea cools faster than the land at night.
the land absorbs more radiation at night.
air over the land is less dense at night.
questions.explanation: Land has a lower specific heat capacity than water; at night the sea is warmer, air rises over it and air from the land flows in.

questions.stem: Cooking pots are often made of aluminium with handles made of wood or plastic because
options: wood and plastic expand more than aluminium.
aluminium is a poor conductor while wood is a good conductor.
aluminium is a good conductor while wood and plastic are poor conductors.
aluminium has a high specific heat capacity.
questions.explanation: The pot must conduct heat to the food quickly; the handle must insulate the cook's hand.

questions.stem: Heat flows by conduction through a wall of area 2 m^2 and thickness 0.1 m. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 0.8 W m^-1 K^-1, and the faces are at 30 degrees C and 20 degrees C. The rate of heat flow is
questions.explanation: Q/t = k A (theta1 - theta2)/x = 0.8 x 2 x 10/0.1 = 160 W.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 600 cm^3 at 27 degrees C. At constant pressure, it is heated until its volume becomes 800 cm^3. Its new temperature is
questions.explanation: Charles's law with absolute temperatures: T2 = 300 x 800/600 = 400 K = 127 degrees C.

questions.stem: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water from 25 degrees C to 75 degrees C? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1)
questions.explanation: Q = m c Delta theta = 2 x 4200 x 50 = 420 000 J.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg block of metal at 100 degrees C is dropped into 0.2 kg of water at 20 degrees C. The final temperature of the mixture is 30 degrees C. Neglecting heat losses and taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, the specific heat capacity of the metal is
questions.explanation: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water: 0.5 x c x 70 = 0.2 x 4200 x 10 = 8400, so c = 240 J kg^-1 K^-1.

questions.stem: During melting, the temperature of a pure solid remains constant because the heat supplied is used to
options: break the bonds between the molecules.
increase the kinetic energy of the molecules.
raise the temperature of the surroundings.
decrease the mass of the solid.
questions.explanation: Latent heat increases the potential energy of the molecules by overcoming intermolecular forces, not their average kinetic energy.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to convert 0.2 kg of ice at 0 degrees C into water at 20 degrees C? (Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1)
Which of the following is TRUE of evaporation but NOT of boiling?
options: It takes place at a fixed temperature for a given pressure.
It takes place throughout the liquid with formation of bubbles.
It takes place at all temperatures and only at the surface of the liquid.
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a definite temperature; evaporation occurs only at the surface at any temperature. Both need latent heat.

questions.stem: A liquid boils at the temperature at which its saturated vapour pressure
options: equals the pressure of the dry air above it.
questions.explanation: Bubbles of vapour can form and grow inside the liquid only when s.v.p. equals the external pressure.

questions.topic: Humidity, relative humidity and dew point
questions.stem: The dew point is the temperature at which
options: the water vapour present in the air is just sufficient to saturate it.
questions.explanation: Cooling air to its dew point makes it saturated, and further cooling causes dew to form.

questions.stem: People feel uncomfortable on hot, humid days in coastal cities such as Lagos mainly because
options: sweat evaporates slowly from the skin when the relative humidity is high.
humid air conducts heat into the body.
questions.explanation: Evaporation of sweat cools the body; when the air is nearly saturated, evaporation is slow and the body cools poorly.

questions.topic: Production and propagation of mechanical waves
questions.stem: A mechanical wave transfers
options: matter from one place to another.
both matter and energy from the source.
energy from one point to another without the medium moving along with it.
questions.explanation: Particles of the medium only vibrate about their mean positions while the energy travels on.

questions.stem: When a stone is dropped into a still pond, circular ripples spread out. A small cork floating on the pond as the ripples pass
options: moves up and down about its position.
moves towards the point where the stone fell.
questions.explanation: The water particles (and the cork) oscillate about mean positions; only the disturbance travels outward.

questions.stem: The distance between two successive crests of a wave is called the
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive points in phase, such as two adjacent crests.

questions.topic: Mathematical relationship connecting f, wavelength, T and v
questions.stem: A wave of frequency 50 Hz travels with a speed of 340 m/s. Its wavelength is
Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
options: Wave on a plucked guitar string
questions.explanation: In sound waves the particles vibrate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions.

questions.stem: A progressive wave is represented by y = 0.04 sin(200 pi t - 0.5 pi x), where x and y are in metres and t in seconds. The wavelength of the wave is
questions.explanation: Comparing with y = A sin(2 pi f t - 2 pi x/lambda): 2 pi/lambda = 0.5 pi, so lambda = 4 m. (f = 100 Hz.)

questions.stem: The bending of waves around the edges of an obstacle is called
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading of waves around obstacles or through gaps comparable in size to the wavelength.

questions.stem: Which of the following properties shows that light waves are transverse?
questions.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised; diffraction, interference and refraction happen with longitudinal waves too.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a luminous object?
questions.explanation: A luminous object produces its own light; the moon, mirrors and paper only reflect light.

questions.stem: A pinhole camera 20 cm long forms an image of a tree 50 m away. If the image is 4 cm high, the height of the tree is
questions.explanation: Magnification = image height/object height = image distance/object distance: h = 4 x 5000/20 cm = 1000 cm = 10 m.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 45 degrees to each other. The number of images formed of an object placed between them is

questions.topic: Reflection of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image distance is
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30, so v = 15 cm (real, in front of the mirror).

questions.topic: Reflection of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem: Convex mirrors are used as driving mirrors in vehicles because they
options: give a wide field of view with erect images.
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors always form erect, diminished virtual images and show a wide area behind the vehicle.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: A ray of light passes from air into glass at an angle of incidence of 45 degrees. If the angle of refraction is 28 degrees, the refractive index of the glass is

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: The critical angle for light passing from a certain glass into air is 40 degrees. The refractive index of the glass is

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: A swimming pool appears to be 1.5 m deep when viewed vertically from above. If the refractive index of water is 4/3, the real depth is
questions.explanation: n = real depth/apparent depth, so real depth = 4/3 x 1.5 = 2.0 m.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object is placed 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. The magnification of the image is

questions.topic: Refraction of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem: An object placed between a converging lens and its principal focus produces an image that is
questions.explanation: With u less than f the rays diverge after the lens; the image is virtual, upright and enlarged, as in a magnifying glass.

questions.topic: Application of lenses in optical instruments
questions.stem: In a compound microscope, the objective and the eyepiece are
options: both converging lenses, the objective having the longer focal length.
a converging objective and a diverging eyepiece.
both converging lenses, the objective having the shorter focal length.
questions.explanation: A compound microscope uses two converging lenses; the objective has a very short focal length. A long-focus objective is used in an astronomical telescope.

questions.topic: Dispersion of white light by a triangular glass prism
questions.stem: When white light passes through a triangular glass prism, the colour that is deviated MOST is
questions.explanation: Glass has the highest refractive index for violet light, so violet is deviated most and red least.

questions.topic: Dispersion of white light by a triangular glass prism
questions.stem: A red shirt viewed in pure green light appears
questions.explanation: A red dye reflects only red light; it absorbs green, so no light is reflected and the shirt looks black.

questions.stem: All electromagnetic waves travel in a vacuum with the same
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists electromagnetic radiations in order of INCREASING wavelength?
options: Radio waves, infrared, visible light, X-rays
Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light
Visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Infrared, microwaves, visible light, radio waves
questions.explanation: From shortest to longest: gamma, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves.

questions.stem: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. Taking the speed of electromagnetic waves as 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, the wavelength of its waves is
The radiation used in TV remote controls and for night-vision cameras is
questions.explanation: Infrared radiation is emitted by warm bodies and is used in remote controls and thermal imaging.

questions.stem: All sounds are produced by
questions.explanation: Sound is produced when a body vibrates, e.g. a drum skin, a string or vocal cords.

questions.topic: Speed of sound in solid, liquid and air
questions.stem: Sound generally travels fastest in
questions.explanation: Sound travels about 5000 m/s in steel, 1500 m/s in water and 340 m/s in air; it cannot travel in a vacuum.

questions.stem: A boy claps his hands while standing 170 m from a tall wall and hears the echo 1.0 s later. The speed of sound is
questions.explanation: The sound travels to the wall and back: v = 2d/t = 340/1.0 = 340 m/s.

questions.stem: A ship sends an ultrasonic pulse to the sea bed and receives the echo 0.8 s later. If the speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s, the depth of the sea is
Two notes of the same pitch and loudness played on a flute and a guitar sound different because they differ in
questions.explanation: Different instruments produce different combinations of overtones with the fundamental, giving different quality.

questions.stem: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 200 Hz. If the tension in the string is quadrupled, its fundamental frequency becomes
questions.explanation: f = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu): f is proportional to sqrt(T), so f becomes 200 x sqrt(4) = 400 Hz.

questions.stem: The sound of a tuning fork becomes louder when its stem is pressed on a table top because
options: the table is set into forced vibration and a larger area of air is disturbed.
the frequency of the fork increases.
the table produces its own natural frequency.
the fork vibrates for a longer time.
questions.explanation: The table top is forced to vibrate at the fork's frequency; its large surface moves more air, increasing loudness.

questions.stem: In a resonance tube experiment, the first resonance with a 512 Hz fork occurs at a length of 16.0 cm of the air column. Neglecting end correction, the speed of sound is
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe at first resonance L = lambda/4, so lambda = 0.64 m and v = 512 x 0.64 = 327.7 m/s.

questions.topic: Vibration of air in pipes: open and closed pipes
questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 150 Hz. Which of the following frequencies can it NOT produce as an overtone?
questions.explanation: A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics: 150, 450, 750, 1050 Hz ... The even harmonic 300 Hz is absent.

questions.topic: Vibration of air in pipes: open and closed pipes
questions.stem: An open pipe 0.85 m long sounds its fundamental note. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, the fundamental frequency is (neglect end correction)
questions.explanation: For an open pipe lambda = 2L = 1.7 m, so f = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz.

questions.stem: Which of the following fields can be either attractive or repulsive?
questions.explanation: Gravitational forces are always attractive; electric (and magnetic) forces can attract or repel depending on the signs of the charges or poles.

questions.stem: The acceleration due to gravity at the earth's surface is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator mainly because
options: the poles are colder than the equator.
the earth's radius is smaller at the poles and the earth rotates.
the poles are closer to the sun.
the earth's magnetic field is stronger at the poles.
questions.explanation: The earth is flattened at the poles (smaller radius) and the rotation effect reduces apparent g at the equator.

questions.topic: Gravitational force between two masses: Newton's law of gravitation
questions.stem: Calculate the gravitational force between two lorries of masses 5 000 kg and 8 000 kg whose centres are 10 m apart. (G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2)
A geostationary communication satellite
options: has an orbital period of about 24 hours and stays above the same point on the equator.
orbits over the poles every 90 minutes.
moves from east to west faster than the earth rotates.
has no gravitational force acting on it.
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane with the same period as the earth's rotation, so it appears fixed in the sky.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit close to the earth's surface. Taking g = 10 m s^-2 and the earth's radius as 6.4 x 10^6 m, its orbital speed is
questions.explanation: For a low orbit, mg = m v^2/R, so v = sqrt(gR) = sqrt(6.4 x 10^7) = 8.0 x 10^3 m/s.

questions.stem: When a polythene rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth, the rod becomes negatively charged because
options: protons are transferred from the rod to the wool.
electrons are transferred from the wool to the rod.
electrons are created in the rod by friction.
neutrons move from the wool to the rod.
questions.explanation: Only electrons move during charging by friction; the rod gains electrons and the wool is left positive.

questions.stem: On a pear-shaped charged conductor, the surface charge density is greatest
questions.explanation: Charge concentrates where the curvature is greatest; this is the basis of point action and lightning conductors.

questions.topic: Electric force between point charges: Coulomb's law
questions.stem: Two point charges of +4 microcoulombs and -3 microcoulombs are 0.3 m apart in air. Taking k = 9.0 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the magnitude of the force between them is
Capacitors of 3 microfarads and 6 microfarads are connected in series. Their effective capacitance is
questions.explanation: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so C = 2 microfarads. (In parallel they would give 9 microfarads.)

questions.stem: The energy stored in a 10 microfarad capacitor charged to 100 V is

questions.topic: Production of electric current from primary and secondary cells
questions.stem: Local action in a simple voltaic cell is caused by
options: hydrogen bubbles collecting on the copper plate.
questions.explanation: Impurities form tiny local cells that dissolve the zinc even when no current is taken; amalgamating zinc prevents it. Hydrogen bubbles cause polarisation.

questions.topic: Production of electric current from primary and secondary cells
questions.stem: Which of the following is a secondary (rechargeable) cell?
questions.explanation: A lead-acid accumulator can be recharged by passing current through it in the reverse direction; the others are primary cells.

questions.stem: A current of 2 A flows through a lamp for 5 minutes. The quantity of charge that passes through the lamp is
A cell of e.m.f. 6 V and internal resistance 1 ohm is connected to a 5 ohm resistor. The terminal potential difference of the cell is
questions.explanation: I = E/(R + r) = 6/6 = 1 A; terminal p.d. = IR = 1 x 5 = 5 V. The lost volts (1 V) are across the internal resistance.

questions.stem: A 2 ohm resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of 3 ohm and 6 ohm resistors across a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 ohm resistor is
questions.explanation: Parallel part = 2 ohms; total = 4 ohms; I = 3 A. p.d. across parallel part = 3 x 2 = 6 V; current in 6 ohms = 6/6 = 1 A.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT obey Ohm's law?
options: A metallic wire at constant temperature
A carbon resistor at constant temperature
questions.explanation: A diode's current does not increase in proportion to voltage and depends on direction; metal conductors at constant temperature are ohmic.

questions.stem: Electric current in an electrolyte such as copper(II) sulphate solution is carried by
questions.explanation: In electrolytes, charge is carried by ions moving in opposite directions; in metals it is carried by free electrons.

questions.stem: A household uses four 60 W bulbs for 5 hours each day. If electricity costs ₦200 per kWh, the cost of lighting for 30 days is
questions.explanation: Energy = 4 x 0.06 kW x 5 h x 30 = 36 kWh; cost = 36 x 200 = ₦7 200.

questions.stem: A galvanometer of resistance 10 ohms gives full-scale deflection with 5 mA. The resistance of the shunt needed to convert it to an ammeter reading up to 1 A is approximately
A wire is stretched uniformly so that its length doubles. Its resistance becomes
questions.explanation: Volume is constant, so doubling L halves A; R = rho L/A increases by 2 x 2 = 4.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, P = 4 ohms, Q = 6 ohms and R = 10 ohms, where P/Q = R/S. The unknown resistance S is
questions.explanation: S = R Q/P = 10 x 6/4 = 15 ohms.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem: In a potentiometer experiment, a standard cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V balances at 60 cm and a second cell balances at 80 cm on the same wire. The e.m.f. of the second cell is
questions.explanation: E is proportional to balance length: E2 = 1.5 x 80/60 = 2.0 V.

questions.topic: Properties of magnets and magnetic materials
questions.stem: The only sure test for magnetism in a steel bar is
questions.explanation: Attraction also occurs between a magnet and unmagnetised iron; only repulsion proves the bar is a magnet.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods will demagnetise a bar magnet most effectively?
options: Keeping it with keepers in a north-south direction
Placing it in a solenoid carrying direct current
Withdrawing it slowly from a solenoid carrying alternating current, with the magnet pointing east-west
questions.explanation: Slow withdrawal from an a.c. solenoid takes the domains through decreasing cycles of magnetisation, leaving them randomly arranged.

questions.stem: Soft iron is used for the core of an electromagnet rather than steel because soft iron
options: is easily magnetised and easily demagnetised.
is a poor conductor of electricity.
questions.explanation: Soft iron has high permeability and low retentivity, so the magnet can be switched off. Steel is used for permanent magnets.

questions.stem: Which of the following materials is diamagnetic?
questions.explanation: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic; copper is weakly repelled by a magnetic field, i.e. diamagnetic.

questions.topic: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor and between parallel conductors
questions.stem: A straight wire 0.5 m long carrying a current of 4 A lies at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.3 T. The force on the wire is

questions.topic: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor and between parallel conductors
questions.stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. The wires
questions.explanation: Currents in the same direction attract; currents in opposite directions repel.

questions.stem: Which of the following devices does NOT make use of an electromagnet?
questions.explanation: A filament lamp simply heats a wire; bells, earpieces and relays all use electromagnets.

questions.stem: At the magnetic equator, the angle of dip is
questions.explanation: At the magnetic equator the earth's field is horizontal, so a freely suspended dip needle rests horizontally. At the magnetic poles dip is 90 degrees.

questions.topic: Magnetic force on a moving charged particle
questions.stem: An electron moving at 2.0 x 10^6 m/s enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T at right angles to the field. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the magnitude of the force on the electron is
The magnetic flux through a coil of 200 turns changes from 0.05 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.2 s. The average e.m.f. induced in the coil is
questions.explanation: E = N Delta(phi)/Delta t = 200 x 0.04/0.2 = 40 V.

questions.stem: A d.c. motor differs from an a.c. generator in that the motor
options: converts mechanical energy to electrical energy.
converts electrical energy to mechanical energy and uses a split-ring commutator.
uses slip rings to reverse the current.
questions.explanation: A motor converts electrical to mechanical energy; its split-ring commutator reverses the coil current every half turn. An a.c. generator uses slip rings.

questions.stem: The S.I. unit of inductance is the
questions.explanation: Inductance is measured in henries (1 H = 1 V s A^-1). Tesla is flux density, weber is flux, farad is capacitance.

questions.stem: Electrical power is transmitted over long distances at very high voltages in order to
options: increase the current in the cables.
reduce the current and hence the I^2R power loss in the cables.
reduce the resistance of the cables.
questions.explanation: For a given power P = VI, high voltage means low current and therefore much smaller heating losses in the lines.

questions.stem: A power station delivers 100 kW through cables of total resistance 2 ohms. The power lost in the cables when the transmission voltage is 10 kV is
The r.m.s. value of an alternating voltage is 220 V. Its peak value is approximately
A 0.1 H inductor of negligible resistance is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Taking pi = 3.14, its inductive reactance is

questions.topic: Series circuit containing resistor, inductor and capacitor
questions.stem: A series circuit contains a resistor of 30 ohms, an inductor of reactance 60 ohms and a capacitor of reactance 20 ohms. The impedance of the circuit is
In a purely capacitive a.c. circuit, the current
options: is in phase with the voltage.
lags behind the voltage by 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: In a capacitor the current leads the voltage by pi/2; in a pure inductor it lags by pi/2; in a resistor they are in phase.

questions.stem: At resonance in a series RLC circuit,
options: the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance and the impedance equals R.
questions.explanation: X_L = X_C, so Z = R, which is the minimum impedance; the current is therefore maximum.

questions.stem: An inductor of 0.4 H and a capacitor of 10 microfarads are connected in series. The resonant frequency of the circuit is approximately
In an a.c. circuit, the r.m.s. voltage is 200 V, the r.m.s. current is 5 A and the phase angle between them is 60 degrees. The average power consumed is
questions.explanation: P = Vrms Irms cos(phi) = 200 x 5 x 0.5 = 500 W.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, the deflection of a few alpha particles through large angles showed that
options: the atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge.
the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through (mostly empty space); a few were strongly repelled by a small, dense, positive nucleus.

questions.stem: A major weakness of the Rutherford model of the atom is that it could not explain
options: the stability of the atom and its line spectra.
questions.explanation: A classical orbiting electron should radiate and spiral into the nucleus; Bohr's quantised orbits explained stability and line spectra.

questions.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from an energy level of -3.4 eV to -13.6 eV. The energy of the photon emitted is
questions.explanation: Photon energy = E2 - E1 = -3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2 eV.

questions.stem: In the photoelectric effect, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons depends on the
questions.explanation: Einstein's equation: KEmax = hf - W. Intensity affects only the number of electrons emitted.

questions.stem: The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. Light of photon energy 3.5 eV falls on it. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is
questions.explanation: KEmax = hf - W = 3.5 - 2.0 = 1.5 eV.

questions.stem: The threshold frequency of a metal is 6.0 x 10^14 Hz. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, its work function is
In an X-ray tube, the target is made of tungsten mainly because tungsten
options: has a high melting point and a high atomic number.
questions.explanation: Most of the electrons' energy becomes heat, so a high melting point is essential; high atomic number gives efficient X-ray production.

questions.stem: Increasing the accelerating voltage across an X-ray tube produces X-rays that are
options: greater in number but equally penetrating.
questions.explanation: Higher accelerating p.d. gives the electrons more energy, producing higher-frequency, shorter-wavelength, harder X-rays. Filament current controls intensity.

questions.stem: The nucleus of an atom of 23/11 Na (mass number 23, atomic number 11) contains
questions.explanation: Protons = atomic number = 11; neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.

questions.stem: Which of the following radiations is deflected by a magnetic field and is stopped by a thin sheet of paper?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are charged (deflected) and have very low penetrating power; gamma and X-rays are not deflected.

questions.stem: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of the original sample remains after 32 days?
questions.explanation: 32 days = 4 half-lives; fraction left = (1/2)^4 = 1/16.

questions.stem: A radioactive nuclide of mass 80 g decays to 5 g in 60 minutes. Its half-life is
questions.explanation: 80 to 5 g is a factor of 16 = 2^4, i.e. 4 half-lives in 60 min, so half-life = 15 min.

questions.stem: A nucleus of 238/92 U (mass number 238, atomic number 92) emits an alpha particle. The mass number and atomic number of the daughter nucleus are
questions.explanation: Alpha emission removes 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number: 234 and 90 (thorium).

questions.stem: When a nucleus emits a beta particle, its
options: atomic number increases by one and its mass number is unchanged.
atomic number and mass number both stay unchanged.
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron changes to a proton and an electron, so Z increases by 1 and A is unchanged.

questions.stem: In a nuclear reaction the mass defect is 2.0 x 10^-28 kg. Taking c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, the energy released is
In a nuclear reactor, the function of the moderator (e.g. graphite or heavy water) is to
options: absorb all the neutrons to stop the reaction.
remove heat from the reactor core.
slow down fast neutrons so that they can cause further fission.
questions.explanation: Slow (thermal) neutrons are more likely to cause fission of U-235. Control rods absorb neutrons; the coolant removes heat.

questions.stem: The diffraction of electrons by a thin crystal shows that electrons
options: travel at the speed of light.
questions.explanation: Diffraction is a wave phenomenon; it confirmed de Broglie's prediction that moving particles have an associated wavelength.

questions.stem: An electron of mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg moves with a speed of 2.0 x 10^6 m/s. Taking h = 6.6 x 10^-34 J s, its de Broglie wavelength is approximately
Which of the following phenomena demonstrates the PARTICLE nature of light?
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect is explained only by light arriving as photons of energy hf; the others are wave effects.

questions.stem: A stone is projected horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Taking g = 10 m s^-2 and neglecting air resistance, the horizontal distance from the foot of the cliff to where it lands is
questions.explanation: Time to fall: 20 = 5t^2, t = 2 s. Range = 15 x 2 = 30 m.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked with a speed of 20 m/s at 30 degrees above the horizontal on level ground. Taking g = 10 m s^-2, its time of flight is
questions.explanation: T = 2u sin(theta)/g = 2 x 20 x 0.5/10 = 2.0 s.

questions.stem: For a projectile launched with a given speed on level ground, the maximum horizontal range is obtained at an angle of projection of
questions.explanation: R = u^2 sin(2 theta)/g is greatest when sin(2 theta) = 1, i.e. theta = 45 degrees.

questions.stem: A spring extends by 4 cm when a load of 20 N is hung on it. Assuming the elastic limit is not exceeded, the extension produced by a load of 35 N is
questions.explanation: Hooke's law: k = 20/4 = 5 N/cm, so extension = 35/5 = 7 cm.

questions.stem: A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 x 10^-6 m^2 stretches by 1.0 mm under a load of 100 N. The Young's modulus of the material is
Light travels along an optical fibre by
options: repeated refraction out of the fibre.
absorption and re-emission at the cladding.
questions.explanation: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so rays striking the boundary beyond the critical angle are totally reflected.

questions.stem: The letters LASER stand for
options: Linear Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Rays
Light Absorption by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Energy Release
questions.explanation: Laser action relies on stimulated emission from a population inversion.

questions.stem: Laser light differs from ordinary light from a filament lamp in that laser light is
questions.explanation: Stimulated emission produces photons of the same frequency, phase and direction.

questions.stem: Adding a small amount of a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus to pure silicon produces
questions.explanation: Each pentavalent atom donates a free electron, so electrons become the majority carriers (n-type). Trivalent impurities give p-type.

questions.stem: A p-n junction diode is forward biased when
options: both sides are connected to the positive terminal.
the n-side is connected to the positive terminal.
the p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery.
questions.explanation: Forward bias reduces the depletion layer and allows current; a reverse-biased diode conducts almost no current.

questions.stem: The electrical resistance of a pure semiconductor such as germanium
questions.explanation: Heating frees more electron-hole pairs, increasing conductivity; metals show the opposite behaviour.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between uniform acceleration and non-uniform acceleration. [2 marks]
(b) A bus starts from rest at a motor park in Ibadan and accelerates uniformly to 18 m/s in 6 s. It travels at this speed for 10 s and is then brought to rest uniformly in 4 s.
(i) Sketch, and describe in words, the velocity-time graph of the motion. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate the acceleration during the first 6 s. [2 marks]
(iii) Calculate the retardation during the last 4 s. [2 marks]
(iv) Calculate the total distance travelled. [4 marks]
(v) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Uniform acceleration: velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals
1 mark: Non-uniform acceleration: velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal time intervals
1 mark: Graph: straight line rising from origin to 18 m/s at t = 6 s
1 mark: Horizontal line at 18 m/s from t = 6 s to t = 16 s
1 mark: Straight line falling to zero at t = 20 s; axes labelled
1 mark: a = (v - u)/t = (18 - 0)/6
1 mark: a = 3 m/s^2
1 mark: Retardation = 18/4
1 mark: = 4.5 m/s^2
1 mark: Distance = area under v-t graph; first stage = 1/2 x 6 x 18 = 54 m
1 mark: Second stage = 18 x 10 = 180 m
1 mark: Third stage = 1/2 x 4 x 18 = 36 m
1 mark: Total = 270 m
1 mark: Average speed = total distance/total time = 270/20
1 mark: = 13.5 m/s
questions.explanation: (a) Uniform acceleration means equal changes of velocity in equal times; non-uniform means unequal changes. (b)(i) Trapezium-shaped v-t graph: rise 0 to 18 m/s over 0-6 s, flat to 16 s, fall to zero at 20 s. (ii) 3 m/s^2. (iii) 4.5 m/s^2. (iv) Area = 54 + 180 + 36 = 270 m. (v) 270/20 = 13.5 m/s.

questions.stem:
(a) What is meant by a projectile? Give two examples of projectile motion in everyday life. [3 marks]
(b) State two assumptions made in the simple theory of projectile motion. [2 marks]
(c) A footballer kicks a ball from level ground with a velocity of 30 m/s at an angle of 30 degrees to the horizontal. Neglecting air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s^2, calculate:
(i) the time taken to reach the maximum height; [3 marks]
(ii) the maximum height reached; [2 marks]
(iii) the time of flight; [2 marks]
(iv) the horizontal range. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: A projectile is a body thrown into the air that moves under the influence of gravity only (after release)
2 marks: Any two examples, 1 mark each: a kicked football, a thrown javelin or stone, a bullet fired from a gun, water from a hose
2 marks: Any two assumptions, 1 mark each: air resistance is negligible; g is constant; horizontal velocity is constant; the earth is flat over the range
1 mark: Vertical component u sin 30 = 30 x 0.5 = 15 m/s
1 mark: At maximum height vertical velocity = 0: t = u sin(theta)/g
1 mark: t = 15/10 = 1.5 s
1 mark: H = (u sin theta)^2/2g = 225/20
1 mark: H = 11.25 m
1 mark: Time of flight = 2 x 1.5
1 mark: = 3.0 s
1 mark: Horizontal component = 30 cos 30 = 25.98 m/s
1 mark: R = 25.98 x 3.0
1 mark: R = 77.9 m (approximately 78 m)
questions.explanation: (a) A projectile is any body given an initial velocity and then left to move under gravity alone, e.g. a kicked football, a thrown javelin. (b) Air resistance neglected; g constant. (c)(i) t = 15/10 = 1.5 s. (ii) H = 15^2/20 = 11.25 m. (iii) 3.0 s. (iv) R = 30 cos 30 x 3.0 = 77.9 m.

questions.topic: Second Law: force, acceleration, momentum and impulse
questions.stem:
(a) State Newton's second law of motion. [2 marks]
(b) State the principle of conservation of linear momentum. [2 marks]
(c) A car of mass 1 500 kg travelling at 20 m/s along the Lagos-Ibadan expressway collides with a stationary car of mass 1 000 kg. The two cars move off together after the collision.
(i) Calculate their common velocity just after the collision. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate the kinetic energy lost in the collision. [4 marks]
(iii) If the collision lasted 0.1 s, calculate the average force exerted on the first car. [2 marks]
(d) Explain why seat belts reduce injuries to passengers in such a collision. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and takes place in the direction of the force
2 marks: When two or more bodies interact, their total momentum remains constant provided no external force acts on them
1 mark: Total momentum before = 1500 x 20 + 0 = 30 000 kg m/s
1 mark: (1500 + 1000)v = 30 000
1 mark: v = 12 m/s
1 mark: KE before = 1/2 x 1500 x 20^2 = 300 000 J
1 mark: KE after = 1/2 x 2500 x 12^2 = 180 000 J
1 mark: Loss = 300 000 - 180 000
1 mark: = 120 000 J (1.2 x 10^5 J)
1 mark: F = change in momentum/time = 1500(20 - 12)/0.1
1 mark: F = 1.2 x 10^5 N
1 mark: The belt stops the passenger moving forward by inertia into the windscreen or dashboard
1 mark: It stretches slightly, increasing the stopping time and so reducing the force (F = change in momentum/time)
questions.explanation: (a) Rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and occurs in its direction. (b) Total momentum of interacting bodies is constant if no external force acts. (c)(i) 30 000/2500 = 12 m/s. (ii) 300 000 - 180 000 = 120 000 J. (iii) 1500 x 8/0.1 = 1.2 x 10^5 N. (d) Belts restrain the body against its inertia and lengthen the stopping time, reducing the force.

questions.stem:
(a) Define the following terms as applied to a machine: (i) mechanical advantage; (ii) velocity ratio; (iii) efficiency. [3 marks]
(b) Give two reasons why the efficiency of a pulley system is always less than 100%. [2 marks]
(c) A block-and-tackle pulley system has two pulleys in each block. It is used at a building site in Enugu to raise a load of 1 200 N through a height of 2 m with an effort of 400 N.
(i) State the velocity ratio of the system. [1 mark]
(ii) Calculate the mechanical advantage. [2 marks]
(iii) Calculate the efficiency. [2 marks]
(iv) Calculate the work done by the effort and the energy wasted. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: M.A. = load/effort
1 mark: V.R. = distance moved by effort/distance moved by load
1 mark: Efficiency = (work output/work input) x 100%
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: friction in the pulley bearings; weight of the lower (moving) block must be lifted; weight/stiffness of the rope
1 mark: V.R. = total number of pulleys = 4
1 mark: M.A. = 1200/400
1 mark: = 3
1 mark: Efficiency = M.A./V.R. x 100% = 3/4 x 100%
1 mark: = 75%
1 mark: Effort moves 4 x 2 = 8 m
1 mark: Work input = 400 x 8 = 3 200 J
1 mark: Work output = 1200 x 2 = 2 400 J
1 mark: Energy wasted = 3200 - 2400
1 mark: = 800 J
questions.explanation: (a) M.A. = load/effort; V.R. = effort distance/load distance; efficiency = work output/work input x 100%. (b) Friction and the weight of the moving block. (c)(i) 4. (ii) 3. (iii) 75%. (iv) Work input 3200 J, useful work 2400 J, wasted 800 J.

questions.stem:
(a) State Archimedes' principle. [2 marks]
(b) State the law of flotation and explain why a steel ship floats although steel is denser than water. [4 marks]
(c) A piece of metal weighs 0.60 N in air, 0.40 N when completely immersed in water and 0.44 N when completely immersed in a liquid X. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg/m^3 and g = 10 m/s^2, calculate:
(i) the upthrust in water; [1 mark]
(ii) the volume of the metal; [3 marks]
(iii) the relative density of the metal; [2 marks]
(iv) the relative density of liquid X. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: When a body is wholly or partially immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced
1 mark: Law of flotation: a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats
1 mark: The ship is hollow/shaped so that it encloses a large volume of air
1 mark: It therefore displaces a large volume of water
1 mark: The weight of water displaced equals the ship's weight before it is fully submerged, so it floats (its average density is less than that of water)
1 mark: Upthrust = 0.60 - 0.40 = 0.20 N
1 mark: Upthrust = V rho g, so V = 0.20/(1000 x 10)
1 mark: V = 2.0 x 10^-5 m^3
1 mark: (i.e. 20 cm^3)
1 mark: R.D. = weight in air/upthrust in water = 0.60/0.20
1 mark: = 3.0
1 mark: Upthrust in X = 0.60 - 0.44 = 0.16 N
1 mark: R.D. of X = upthrust in X/upthrust in water = 0.16/0.20
1 mark: = 0.80
questions.explanation: (a) Upthrust on an immersed body equals the weight of fluid displaced. (b) A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid; a hollow steel ship displaces a large volume of water whose weight equals the ship's weight. (c)(i) 0.20 N. (ii) 2.0 x 10^-5 m^3. (iii) 3.0. (iv) 0.16/0.20 = 0.80.

questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem:
(a) Define simple harmonic motion. [2 marks]
(b) Define the following terms for an oscillating body: (i) amplitude; (ii) period; (iii) frequency. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the period of a simple pendulum of length 40 cm at a place where g = 9.8 m/s^2. [3 marks]
(d) In an experiment, a student in Kano obtains a period of 2.2 s for a pendulum of length 1.2 m. Calculate the value of g obtained. [3 marks]
(e) State two precautions the student should take to obtain an accurate value of the period. [2 marks]
(f) State two examples of bodies that perform simple harmonic motion. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Motion in which the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards that point
1 mark: Amplitude: maximum displacement from the equilibrium position
1 mark: Period: time for one complete oscillation
1 mark: Frequency: number of complete oscillations per second
1 mark: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g)
1 mark: = 2 x 3.142 x sqrt(0.40/9.8)
1 mark: = 1.27 s
1 mark: g = 4 pi^2 L/T^2
1 mark: = 4 x 9.87 x 1.2/(2.2)^2
1 mark: = 9.79 m/s^2
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: time at least 20 oscillations and divide; use small amplitude (angle less than about 10 degrees); avoid parallax/start timing at the centre of swing; ensure rigid support/no draughts
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: simple pendulum; mass on a spring; vibrating tuning-fork prong; loaded test tube bobbing in water; vibrating guitar string
questions.explanation: (a) S.H.M.: acceleration proportional to displacement from a fixed point and directed towards it. (b) Amplitude is the maximum displacement; period the time for one oscillation; frequency the number of oscillations per second. (c) T = 2 pi sqrt(0.40/9.8) = 1.27 s. (d) g = 4 pi^2 x 1.2/4.84 = 9.79 m/s^2. (e) Time many oscillations, use small amplitude. (f) Pendulum, mass on spring.

questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) specific heat capacity; (ii) specific latent heat of fusion. [4 marks]
(b) Using the kinetic theory, explain why the temperature of melting ice remains constant although heat is being supplied. [2 marks]
(c) A 200 W immersion heater is used to convert 50 g of ice at 0 degrees C into water at 30 degrees C. Neglecting heat losses and the heat capacity of the container, calculate:
(i) the heat required to melt the ice; [2 marks]
(ii) the heat required to raise the temperature of the melted ice to 30 degrees C; [2 marks]
(iii) the time taken by the heater. [3 marks]
(Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.36 x 10^5 J/kg; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg K)
(d) State two applications of the high specific heat capacity of water. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Specific heat capacity: quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a substance by 1 K
2 marks: Specific latent heat of fusion: quantity of heat required to change unit mass of a solid at its melting point to liquid without change of temperature
1 mark: The heat supplied is used to break the intermolecular bonds/increase the potential energy of the molecules
1 mark: The average kinetic energy of the molecules (and so the temperature) does not increase
1 mark: Q1 = mL = 0.05 x 3.36 x 10^5
1 mark: = 16 800 J
1 mark: Q2 = mc(theta) = 0.05 x 4200 x 30
1 mark: = 6 300 J
1 mark: Total heat = 16 800 + 6 300 = 23 100 J
1 mark: t = heat/power = 23 100/200
1 mark: t = 115.5 s
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: coolant in car radiators; hot-water bottles/central heating; moderation of coastal climate (land and sea breezes)
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Heat to raise 1 kg by 1 K. (ii) Heat to melt 1 kg at its melting point without temperature change. (b) Energy goes into breaking bonds (potential energy), not increasing kinetic energy. (c)(i) 16 800 J. (ii) 6 300 J. (iii) 23 100/200 = 115.5 s. (d) Car radiator coolant; hot-water bottles.

questions.stem:
(a) State (i) Boyle's law; (ii) Charles's law. [4 marks]
(b) Explain, using the kinetic theory, why the pressure of a gas in a closed container increases when it is heated at constant volume. [3 marks]
(c) A fixed mass of gas occupies 400 cm^3 at a pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa and a temperature of 27 degrees C.
(i) Calculate its volume if the pressure is raised to 1.6 x 10^5 Pa at constant temperature. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate its pressure when its volume becomes 500 cm^3 and its temperature 87 degrees C. [4 marks]
(d) Why must temperatures be expressed in kelvin in gas law calculations? [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Boyle's law: the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure provided the temperature is constant
2 marks: Charles's law: the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature provided the pressure is constant
1 mark: Heating increases the average kinetic energy/speed of the molecules
1 mark: The molecules collide with the walls more frequently
1 mark: and with greater force (rate of change of momentum), so pressure increases
1 mark: p1V1 = p2V2
1 mark: V2 = 1.0 x 10^5 x 400/1.6 x 10^5
1 mark: V2 = 250 cm^3
1 mark: T1 = 300 K and T2 = 360 K
1 mark: p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2
1 mark: p2 = 1.0 x 10^5 x 400 x 360/(300 x 500)
1 mark: p2 = 9.6 x 10^4 Pa
1 mark: The gas laws are proportionalities that hold only on the absolute (kelvin) scale, which starts from absolute zero
questions.explanation: (a) Boyle: pV constant at constant T. Charles: V proportional to absolute T at constant p. (b) Faster molecules hit the walls more often and harder. (c)(i) 250 cm^3. (ii) p2 = 9.6 x 10^4 Pa. (d) The laws are proportional only to absolute temperature.

questions.stem:
(a) Define linear expansivity of a solid and state its S.I. unit. [3 marks]
(b) Describe briefly how a bimetallic strip is used in a thermostat to control the temperature of an electric pressing iron. [4 marks]
(c) A steel bridge is 50 m long. Calculate the increase in its length when the temperature rises from 20 degrees C to 60 degrees C. (Linear expansivity of steel = 1.2 x 10^-5 per K) [3 marks]
(d) State two ways in which engineers allow for expansion in bridges and roads. [2 marks]
(e) State three disadvantages of thermal expansion. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Linear expansivity: the increase in length per unit length per degree (kelvin) rise in temperature
1 mark: Unit: per kelvin (K^-1)
1 mark: A bimetallic strip is made of two metals of different expansivities (e.g. brass and invar) riveted together
1 mark: When it is heated, the strip bends because one metal expands more than the other
1 mark: At the set temperature it bends away from the contact and breaks the heating circuit
1 mark: On cooling it straightens, closes the contact and the heater comes on again, keeping the temperature steady
1 mark: Delta L = alpha L0 Delta theta
1 mark: = 1.2 x 10^-5 x 50 x 40
1 mark: = 0.024 m (24 mm)
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: expansion gaps/joints; rollers at one end of a bridge; gaps filled with pitch/bitumen in concrete roads
3 marks: Any three, 1 mark each: buckling of railway lines; cracking of thick glass with hot water; sagging of overhead cables in hot weather; cracking of concrete roads; loosening of clock pendulum timing
questions.explanation: (a) Increase in length per unit original length per kelvin, unit K^-1. (b) The strip bends on heating, opening contacts at the set temperature and closing them on cooling. (c) 0.024 m. (d) Expansion gaps and rollers. (e) Buckling of rails, cracking of glass, sagging wires.

questions.topic: Mathematical relationship connecting f, wavelength, T and v
questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves, giving one example of each. [4 marks]
(b) Define (i) wavelength; (ii) frequency; (iii) amplitude. [3 marks]
(c) Show that the speed v of a wave is related to its frequency f and wavelength lambda by v = f lambda. [3 marks]
(d) A loudspeaker at a school assembly emits a note of frequency 550 Hz. If the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s, calculate:
(i) the wavelength of the note; [2 marks]
(ii) the period of the wave. [2 marks]
(e) State one property that is common to all waves. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Transverse: particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation
1 mark: Example: light/water ripples/waves on a string
1 mark: Longitudinal: particles vibrate parallel to (along) the direction of propagation
1 mark: Example: sound waves/compression waves in a spring
1 mark: Wavelength: distance between two successive particles in phase (e.g. two crests)
1 mark: Frequency: number of complete waves (oscillations) produced per second
1 mark: Amplitude: maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position
1 mark: In one period T the wave travels one wavelength lambda
1 mark: v = distance/time = lambda/T
1 mark: Since f = 1/T, v = f lambda
1 mark: lambda = v/f = 330/550
1 mark: = 0.60 m
1 mark: T = 1/f = 1/550
1 mark: = 1.82 x 10^-3 s
1 mark: Any one: reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference (all waves transfer energy)
questions.explanation: (a) Transverse: vibration perpendicular to travel (light); longitudinal: vibration along travel (sound). (b) Definitions as given. (c) One wavelength travels in one period: v = lambda/T = f lambda. (d)(i) 0.60 m. (ii) 1.82 x 10^-3 s. (e) Reflection.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem:
(a) State the laws of refraction of light. [2 marks]
(b) A ray of light travelling in air strikes a glass block at an angle of incidence of 50 degrees and is refracted at an angle of 30 degrees. Calculate (i) the refractive index of the glass; (ii) the critical angle of the glass. [5 marks]
(c) An object 2 cm tall is placed 20 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15 cm.
(i) Calculate the position of the image. [3 marks]
(ii) Calculate the magnification and the height of the image. [3 marks]
(iii) State two characteristics of the image. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane
1 mark: Snell's law: sin i/sin r is a constant for a given pair of media
1 mark: n = sin i/sin r = sin 50/sin 30
1 mark: = 0.766/0.5 = 1.53
1 mark: sin C = 1/n
1 mark: = 1/1.53 = 0.653
1 mark: C = 40.7 degrees (about 41 degrees)
1 mark: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, so 1/v = 1/15 - 1/20
1 mark: 1/v = 1/60
1 mark: v = 60 cm on the other side of the lens
1 mark: m = v/u = 60/20
1 mark: = 3
1 mark: Image height = 3 x 2 = 6 cm
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: real; inverted; magnified (3 times); formed on the opposite side of the lens
questions.explanation: (a) Incident ray, refracted ray and normal are coplanar; sin i/sin r is constant. (b)(i) 1.53. (ii) C = 40.7 degrees. (c)(i) v = 60 cm. (ii) m = 3, image 6 cm tall. (iii) Real, inverted, magnified.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the term resonance. [2 marks]
(b) Distinguish between a fundamental note and an overtone. [2 marks]
(c) In a resonance tube experiment, a tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz gives the first resonance when the length of the air column is 15.5 cm and the second resonance at 48.5 cm. Calculate:
(i) the wavelength of the sound; [3 marks]
(ii) the speed of sound in air; [2 marks]
(iii) the end correction of the tube. [3 marks]
(d) Explain why a pipe closed at one end produces only odd harmonics. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Resonance occurs when a body is set into vibration at its own natural frequency by another vibrating body, giving maximum amplitude (loud sound)
1 mark: Fundamental: the lowest frequency note produced by a vibrating system
1 mark: Overtone: a note of higher frequency than the fundamental produced together with it
1 mark: Second resonance - first resonance = lambda/2
1 mark: lambda/2 = 48.5 - 15.5 = 33.0 cm
1 mark: lambda = 66.0 cm = 0.66 m
1 mark: v = f lambda = 512 x 0.66
1 mark: = 338 m/s
1 mark: First resonance: l1 + e = lambda/4
1 mark: e = 16.5 - 15.5
1 mark: e = 1.0 cm
1 mark: The closed end must always be a node and the open end an antinode
1 mark: So the pipe length must be an odd number of quarter wavelengths: L = lambda/4, 3 lambda/4, 5 lambda/4 ...
1 mark: Hence the frequencies are f0, 3f0, 5f0 ... (odd harmonics only)
questions.explanation: (a) Vibration at natural frequency driven by another body, giving maximum amplitude. (b) Fundamental is the lowest note; overtones are higher notes produced with it. (c)(i) lambda = 2(48.5 - 15.5) = 66 cm. (ii) 512 x 0.66 = 338 m/s. (iii) e = 16.5 - 15.5 = 1.0 cm. (d) Closed end node, open end antinode, so L = odd multiples of lambda/4.

questions.topic: Gravitational force between two masses: Newton's law of gravitation
questions.stem:
(a) State Newton's law of universal gravitation. [2 marks]
(b) Show that the acceleration due to gravity g at the surface of the earth is related to the mass M and radius R of the earth by g = GM/R^2. [3 marks]
(c) Taking G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2, the mass of the earth as 6.0 x 10^24 kg and its radius as 6.4 x 10^6 m, calculate:
(i) the acceleration due to gravity at the earth's surface; [2 marks]
(ii) the escape velocity from the earth's surface. [3 marks]
(d) What is a geostationary satellite? State two uses of artificial satellites. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
1 mark: Weight of mass m at the surface = mg
1 mark: Gravitational force = GMm/R^2
1 mark: Equating, mg = GMm/R^2, so g = GM/R^2
1 mark: g = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 6.0 x 10^24/(6.4 x 10^6)^2
1 mark: g = 9.77 m/s^2
1 mark: v = sqrt(2GM/R)
1 mark: = sqrt(2 x 6.67 x 10^-11 x 6.0 x 10^24/6.4 x 10^6)
1 mark: v = 1.12 x 10^4 m/s (11.2 km/s)
1 mark: A satellite that orbits above the equator with a period of 24 hours
1 mark: moving in the same direction as the earth's rotation
1 mark: so that it remains above the same point on the earth
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: telecommunication/satellite TV; weather forecasting; GPS navigation; remote sensing/mapping; scientific research
questions.explanation: (a) F = G m1 m2/r^2 between any two masses. (b) mg = GMm/R^2 gives g = GM/R^2. (c)(i) 9.77 m/s^2. (ii) v = sqrt(2GM/R) = 1.12 x 10^4 m/s. (d) A satellite with a 24-hour equatorial orbit that stays over one point; used for communication and weather forecasting.

questions.stem:
(a) Define capacitance and state its S.I. unit. [3 marks]
(b) State three factors that affect the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor. [3 marks]
(c) A 3 microfarad capacitor and a 6 microfarad capacitor are connected in series. This combination is connected in parallel with a 2 microfarad capacitor and the arrangement is connected to a 12 V battery. Calculate:
(i) the effective capacitance of the arrangement; [3 marks]
(ii) the total charge stored; [2 marks]
(iii) the total energy stored. [2 marks]
(d) State two uses of capacitors. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Capacitance is the ratio of the charge on either plate to the potential difference between the plates (C = Q/V)
1 mark: Unit: farad (F)
1 mark: 1 F = 1 C/V
3 marks: Any three, 1 mark each: area of overlap of the plates; distance between the plates; nature (permittivity) of the dielectric
1 mark: Series part: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, C = 2 microfarads
1 mark: Parallel with 2 microfarads: C = 2 + 2
1 mark: = 4 microfarads
1 mark: Q = CV = 4 x 10^-6 x 12
1 mark: = 4.8 x 10^-5 C
1 mark: W = 1/2 CV^2 = 0.5 x 4 x 10^-6 x 144
1 mark: = 2.88 x 10^-4 J
2 marks: Any two, 1 mark each: smoothing in rectifier circuits; tuning radio receivers; storing charge in camera flash units; blocking d.c./passing a.c.; timing circuits
questions.explanation: (a) C = Q/V, unit farad. (b) Plate area, separation, dielectric. (c)(i) 2 + 2 = 4 microfarads. (ii) 4.8 x 10^-5 C. (iii) 2.88 x 10^-4 J. (d) Smoothing, tuning.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between the e.m.f. of a cell and the terminal potential difference. [2 marks]
(b) A battery of e.m.f. 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.5 ohm is connected to a 2.5 ohm resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor. Calculate:
(i) the effective external resistance; [3 marks]
(ii) the current supplied by the battery; [2 marks]
(iii) the terminal potential difference of the battery; [2 marks]
(iv) the power dissipated in the 3 ohm resistor. [3 marks]
(c) Describe briefly how a potentiometer can be used to compare the e.m.f.s of two cells. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: E.m.f.: the p.d. across the terminals of a cell when it is not delivering current (open circuit), or energy supplied per unit charge
1 mark: Terminal p.d.: the p.d. across the terminals when the cell delivers current; it is less than the e.m.f. by the lost volts Ir
1 mark: Parallel part: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, R = 2 ohms
1 mark: External resistance = 2 + 2.5
1 mark: = 4.5 ohms
1 mark: I = E/(R + r) = 9.0/(4.5 + 0.5)
1 mark: I = 1.8 A
1 mark: V = IR = 1.8 x 4.5
1 mark: V = 8.1 V
1 mark: P.d. across parallel part = 1.8 x 2 = 3.6 V
1 mark: P = V^2/R = 3.6^2/3
1 mark: P = 4.32 W
